segments.text: Who was Judas Iscariot? The sources agree on a small core and disagree on almost everything that makes him psychologically familiar.
segments.tts_text: Who was [Judas Iscariot](/ˈdʒuːdəs ɪsˈkæriət/)? The sources agree on a small core and disagree on almost everything that makes him psychologically familiar.

segments.text: Paul’s letters, the earliest surviving Christian writings, never name Judas. First Corinthians says Jesus was “handed over,” but Paul does not identify the person responsible.
segments.tts_text: Paul’s letters, the earliest surviving Christian writings, never name Judas. First Corinthians says Jesus was “handed over,” but Paul does not identify the person responsible.

segments.text: Mark gives us the first surviving narrative. Judas is “one of the Twelve.” He goes to the chief priests, who promise money. Mark gives no amount and no motive. Judas later identifies Jesus with a kiss.

segments.text: Matthew adds thirty pieces of silver, remorse, a returned payment, hanging, and a potter’s field.
segments.tts_text: Matthew adds thirty pieces of silver, remorse, a returned payment, hanging, and a potter’s field.

segments.text: Luke says Satan entered Judas. Acts says Judas acquired a field with the reward, fell headlong, and burst open. The field, buyer, and death account differ materially from Matthew.

segments.text: John adds an even darker portrait: Judas is called a devil and a thief who kept the common purse; Satan enters him; and no kiss is needed when Jesus is arrested.

segments.text: These are not four independent biographies. Matthew and Luke use Mark. John is later and strongly theological. Later detail may preserve history, but it cannot be counted automatically as another independent witness.

segments.text: Even “Iscariot” is unresolved. “Man of Kerioth” is possible, not established.

segments.text: The strongest historical core is narrow: Judas was a Jewish member of the Twelve who helped hand Jesus over for arrest. His motive remains unknown.

segments.text: The second-century Gospel of Judas is not his memoir. It is a later Christian argument whose portrait of Judas remains debated.

segments.text: Judas must never become a symbol of Jewish greed or collective guilt. Jesus, Judas, and the Twelve were Jewish. Rome executed Jesus.

segments.text: What occurred: Judas belonged to the Twelve and enabled the arrest.

segments.text: What survived: increasingly elaborate and conflicting portraits.

segments.text: What no one could know: his private motive and inner experience.
